content: Competence in analytical toxicology should be reassessed periodically, such as every two years, to ensure ongoing proficiency. Training programs must include both practical and theoretical components tailored to the specific needs of the service, as well as the available equipment and facilities. The duration of training may vary depending on the individual’s prior education and experience. Whenever feasible, training should culminate in a recognized qualification. Practical, on-the-job experience is essential, particularly as the scope of analytical toxicology services expands. Continuing education should be actively encouraged, including participation in research and development projects, case presentations, and attendance at international conferences. Membership in national and international toxicological and pharmacological societies should also be promoted. The training requirements for laboratory heads will depend on local circumstances. In countries lacking suitable training programs, assistance should be sought from nations with well-established analytical toxicology services, which can provide training fellowships. In cases where additional expertise is required in specific fields, experts from other countries may be invited to deliver the necessary training. Laboratories providing training in analytical toxicology should meet specific criteria. The head of the laboratory should possess appropriate experience in clinical analytical toxicology, ideally holding a doctorate, having published original research, and possessing teaching experience. Ideally, at least two experienced analytical toxicologists should also be part of the laboratory team to ensure comprehensive coverage. The laboratory should be associated with a multifunctional poison center that provides both information and patient care, facilitating collaboration between clinical and analytical services. It may also offer a 24-hour emergency service. Training should cover good laboratory practices, quality assurance procedures, basic pathology related to clinical toxicology, toxicokinetics, metabolism, human toxicology of analyzed substances, laboratory management, and teaching or oral presentation of cases and research findings. Laboratory staff should be encouraged to engage in continuing professional development, including regular meetings at poison control centers to review case reports, discuss the medical interpretation of analytical results with clinical personnel, and examine developments in analytical toxicology. They should also evaluate research results to identify areas for further investigation and discuss laboratory management in the context of poison control work. Staff should be encouraged to present papers and participate in scientific meetings relevant to their work. Establishing an analytical toxicology service requires significant investment and planning. It is important to determine whether a new laboratory is necessary or if the services of an existing laboratory can be expanded. Sustainability of the laboratory service must also be ensured. Challenges include recruiting and retaining trained, motivated personnel, ensuring a reliable supply of high-quality reagents and consumables, and covering the costs of maintaining and upgrading laboratory equipment. Analytical toxicology services play a critical role in managing poisoning cases and investigating the health effects of chemical exposures. These services are essential for public health and require collaboration among poison centers, toxicology laboratories, public health agencies, and other stakeholders.
